claim: zGrad efficiently degrades transmembrane, cytosolic and nuclear GFP-tagged proteins in zebrafish in an inducible and reversible manner.
source: We named this system zGrad and show that zGrad efficiently degrades transmembrane, cytosolic and nuclear GFP-tagged proteins in zebrafish in an inducible and reversible manner.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing degradation of different protein types.

claim: Global protein depletion by zGrad results in phenotypes similar to loss of gene activity.
source: Global protein depletion results in phenotypes similar to loss of gene activity, while local and temporal protein inactivation yields more restricted and novel phenotypes.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion, which is supported by experimental data showing that zGrad-mediated protein depletion recapitulates genetic loss-of-function phenotypes.

claim: Local and temporal protein inactivation by zGrad yields more restricted and novel phenotypes.
source: Global protein depletion results in phenotypes similar to loss of gene activity, while local and temporal protein inactivation yields more restricted and novel phenotypes.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by experiments showing tissue-specific and temporal protein depletion effects.

claim: OsTIR1-mCherry induces degradation of sfGFP-mAID in a dose-dependent manner irrespective of IAA.
source: We found that expression of OsTIR1-mCherry induced degradation of sfGFP-mAID in a dose-dependent manner irrespective of IAA (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text references Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing dose-dependent degradation without auxin requirement.

claim: 50 pg/embryo or higher concentrations of OsTIR1-mCherry mRNA led to deformed and dying embryos.
source: We also found that 50 pg/embryo or higher concentrations of OsTIR1-mCherry mRNA led to deformed and dying embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The text references figures showing embryo toxicity at high OsTIR1 concentrations.

claim: The AID system is not suitable to degrade proteins in zebrafish in its current form.
source: Thus, low levels of OsTIR1 induce degradation of AID-tagged proteins, higher levels of OsTIR1 are toxic and OsTIR degrades AID-tagged proteins in the absence of auxin, suggesting that, in its current form, the AID system is not suitable to degrade proteins in zebrafish.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data showing toxicity and lack of auxin-dependence.

claim: The ZIF-1/ZF1 tag degradation system only reduced the levels of sfGFP-ZF1 by 17%.
source: We found that the ZIF-1/ZF1 tag degradation only reduced the levels of sfGFP-ZF1 by 17% (Figure 1E,H), indicating that the ZIF-1/ZF1 tag degradation system does not efficiently degrade ZF1-tagged proteins in zebrafish.
evidence: The text references Figure 1E,H showing quantification of degradation efficiency.

claim: Ab-SPOP efficiently degraded nuclear sfGFP-ZF1 (70% reduction) but not cytoplasmic sfGFP-ZF1 (13% reduction).
source: Consistent with the initial description (Shin et al., 2015), Ab-SPOP efficiently degraded nuclear sfGFP-ZF1 (70% reduction, Figure 1F,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) but not cytoplasmic sfGFP-ZF1 (13% reduction, Figure 1F,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text references figures showing differential degradation in nuclear vs. cytoplasmic compartments, with citation to prior work.

claim: The Ab-SPOP/FP-tag degradation system is not suitable for the degradation of non-nuclear proteins in zebrafish.
source: As reported previously (Shin et al., 2015), this confirms that the Ab-SPOP/FP-tag degradation system degrades nuclear proteins efficiently but is not suitable for the degradation of non-nuclear proteins in zebrafish.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data and cites prior work by Shin et al., 2015.

claim: deGradFP reduced sfGFP-ZF1 only slightly (19% reduction).
source: We found that deGradFP reduced sfGFP-ZF1 only slightly (19% reduction, Figure 1G,H).
evidence: The text references Figure 1G,H showing quantification of deGradFP-mediated degradation.

claim: The zebrafish F-box and WD repeat domain containing 11b (fbxw11b) gene is the Drosophila slmb orthologue.
source: Based on sequence homology, we identified the zebrafish F-box and WD repeat domain containing 11b (fbxw11b) gene as the Drosophila slmb orthologue.
evidence: The identification is based on sequence homology analysis.

claim: zGrad depleted sfGFP-ZF1 in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus by 89%.
source: In contrast to deGradFP, which depleted 19% of sfGFP-ZF1, zGrad depleted sfGFP-ZF1 in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus by 89% (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: The text references Figure 1G,H showing quantification of zGrad-mediated degradation.

claim: Degradation of sfGFP-ZF1 by zGrad was observed already at 2.5 hpf.
source: Importantly, we observed degradation of sfGFP-ZF1 by zGrad already at 2.5 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The text references a figure showing early degradation timing.

claim: H2A-EGFP degradation was discernible in zGrad-expressing embryos within 2-3 hr post heat shock.
source: Compared to control embryos that did not carry the hsp70l:zGrad transgene, H2A-EGFP degradation was discernible in zGrad-expressing embryos within 2-3 hr post heat shock in all tissues that expressed nuclear EGFP from the cxcr4b promoter (skin, pronephros, somites, neural tube and primordium, Figure 2A–E, Figure 2—Video 1).
evidence: The text references figures showing time-course of H2A-EGFP degradation.

claim: In the somites, the levels of H2A-EGFP was decreased by 87%.
source: In the somites, the levels of H2A-EGFP was decreased by 87% (Figure 2C), while in the primordium, the levels of H2A-EGFP was decreased by 22% (Figure 2E).
evidence: The text references Figure 2C showing quantification of H2A-EGFP degradation in somites.

claim: In the primordium, the levels of H2A-EGFP was decreased by 22%.
source: In the somites, the levels of H2A-EGFP was decreased by 87% (Figure 2C), while in the primordium, the levels of H2A-EGFP was decreased by 22% (Figure 2E).
evidence: The text references Figure 2E showing quantification of H2A-EGFP degradation in primordium.

claim: The more efficient degradation of H2A-EGFP in the somites than in the primordium is probably due to the lower levels of H2A-EGFP and the lack of H2A-EGFP production in the somites at the time of zGrad induction.
source: The more efficient degradation of H2A-EGFP in the somites than in the primordium is probably due to the lower levels of H2A-EGFP and the lack of H2A-EGFP production in the somites at the time of zGrad induction (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2) (Chong et al., 2001).
evidence: The explanation is based on data from supplementary figures and cited literature (Chong et al., 2001).

claim: The time for onset of degradation and half-life for H2A-EGFP in the somites was 200 min and 156 min, respectively.
source: The time for onset of degradation and half-life for H2A-EGFP in the somites was 200 min and 156 min, respectively (Figure 2C, Table 1).
evidence: The text references Figure 2C and Table 1 showing degradation kinetics.

claim: The time for onset of degradation and the half-life for H2A-EGFP degradation in the primordium was 140 min and 29 min, respectively.
source: The time for onset of degradation and the half-life for H2A-EGFP degradation in the primordium was 140 min and 29 min, respectively (Figure 2E, Table 1).
evidence: The text references Figure 2E and Table 1 showing degradation kinetics.

claim: Cdh1-sfGFP and Cdh1-TagRFP transgenes recapitulated the endogenous Cdh1 expression pattern and rescued the lethality of cdh1 mutant embryos.
source: These transgenes recapitulated the endogenous Cdh1 expression pattern and rescued the lethality of cdh1 mutant embryos (Table 2), indicating that Cdh1-sfGFP and Cdh1-TagRFP are functional.
evidence: The text references Table 2 showing rescue data, indicating functional transgenes.

claim: In zGrad-expressing embryos, Cdh1-sfGFP degradation was uniformly detected within 15 min post heat shock in the skin of the embryo.
source: In zGrad-expressing embryos, Cdh1-sfGFP degradation was uniformly detected within 15 min post heat shock in the skin of the embryo (enveloping layer and epidermal basal layer) (Figure 2F–H, Figure 2—Video 2).
evidence: The text references figures showing rapid Cdh1-sfGFP degradation timing.

claim: zGrad expression reduced the levels of Cdh1-sfGFP in the primordium by 79% with a degradation half-life of 24 min.
source: This analysis showed that zGrad expression reduced the levels of Cdh1-sfGFP in the primordium by 79% with a degradation half-life of 24 min (Figure 2H).
evidence: The text references Figure 2H showing quantification of Cdh1-sfGFP degradation.

claim: The time for onset of Cdh1-sfGFP degradation was 75 min.
source: The time for onset of Cdh1-sfGFP degradation was 75 min (Table 1).
evidence: The text references Table 1 showing degradation kinetics.

claim: Homozygous ctnna:ctnna-Citrine fish are viable, indicating that Ctnna-Citrine is functional.
source: Homozygous ctnna:ctnna-Citrine fish are viable, indicating that Ctnna-Citrine is functional (Trinh et al., 2011).
evidence: The viability of homozygous fish indicates functionality, with citation to Trinh et al., 2011.

claim: The time for onset of degradation of Ctnna-Citrine was 65 min and Ctnna-Citrine was degraded by 58% with a half-life of 19 min in zGrad-expressing embryos.
source: This analysis showed that the time for onset of degradation of Ctnna-Citrine was 65 min and that Ctnna-Citrine was degraded by 58% with a half-life of 19 min in zGrad-expressing embryos (Figure 2K, Table 1).
evidence: The text references Figure 2K and Table 1 showing degradation kinetics.

claim: Expression of zGrad did not degrade secreted GFP.
source: Unlike H2A-EGFP, Cdh1-sfGFP and Ctnna-Citrine, expression of zGrad did not degrade secreted GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The text references a figure showing lack of secreted GFP degradation.

claim: zGrad targets nuclear, cytoplasmic, and transmembrane proteins tagged with EGFP or Citrine for degradation.
source: Together, these observations indicate that zGrad targets nuclear, cytoplasmic, and transmembrane proteins tagged with EGFP or Citrine for degradation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing degradation of proteins in different cellular compartments.

claim: In zGrad mRNA-injected MZ ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos the cells started to become detached and partly shed from the embryo resulting in embryonic lethality around 3 to 5 hpf.
source: In zGrad mRNA-injected MZ ctnna:ctnna-Citrine and M ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos the cells started to become detached and partly shed from the embryo resulting in embryonic lethality around 3 to 5 hpf (Figure 3B,C,E,F).
evidence: The text references figures showing cell detachment and lethality phenotypes.

claim: In zGrad mRNA-injected Z ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos, cells detached from the embryo by 24 hpf and about half of the embryos died.
source: Similarly but delayed by 20 hr, in zGrad mRNA-injected Z ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos, cells detached from the embryo by 24 hpf and about half of the embryos died (note, half the embryos were zygotically homozygous for ctnna:ctnna-Citrine since we crossed ctnna:ctnna-Citrine/ctnna:ctnna-Citrine males to ctnna:ctnna-Citrine/+ females, Figure 3G,H,I) while control injected embryos were unaffected (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: The text references figures showing delayed phenotype in zygotic embryos.

claim: The observed phenotype in Z ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos injected with zGrad mRNA is similar to the defects reported for zygotic ctnna-/- embryos.
source: The observed phenotype in Z ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos injected with zGrad mRNA is similar to the defects reported for zygotic ctnna-/- embryos (Han et al., 2016).
evidence: The comparison is based on experimental data and cites Han et al., 2016.

claim: Maternally supplied Ctnna can sustain cell-cell adhesion and embryonic development for about 1 day before the embryo requires zygotic Ctnna.
source: Moreover, it suggests that maternally supplied Ctnna can sustain cell-cell adhesion and embryonic development for about 1 day before the embryo requires zygotic Ctnna.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the timing difference between maternal and zygotic phenotypes.

claim: cdh1-/-; cdh1:cdh1-sfGFP/+; hsp70l:zGrad/+ embryos shed their skin and rapidly died.
source: In contrast to control embryos which showed no visible defects (Figure 4B,C), we found cdh1-/-; cdh1:cdh1-sfGFP/+; hsp70l:zGrad/+ embryos shed their skin and rapidly died (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the idea that zGrad-mediated Cdh1-sfGFP degradation disrupts the cell-cell adhesion between the skin cells of the embryos that lack endogenous Cdh1 function.
evidence: The text references figures showing skin shedding and lethality phenotypes.

claim: The skin phenotype in embryos with depletion of Cdh1-sfGFP was not always fully penetrant.
source: We would like to note that the skin phenotype in embryos with depletion of Cdh1-sfGFP was not always fully penetrant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text references a figure showing variable penetrance.

claim: Transient expression of zGrad can efficiently degrade GFP-tagged proteins and, if GFP-tagged proteins are depleted sufficiently, cause loss-of-protein function and uncover phenotypes past the initial requirements of essential proteins.
source: In summary, these observations suggest that transient expression of zGrad can efficiently degrade GFP-tagged proteins and, if GFP-tagged proteins are depleted sufficiently, cause loss-of-protein function and uncover phenotypes past the initial requirements of essential proteins.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing phenotypes from protein depletion.

claim: Induction of zGrad degraded Cxcr4b-EGFP and resulted in rounded primordium morphology and stalled primordium migration 90 min after heat shock.
source: This analysis showed that induction of zGrad degraded Cxcr4b-EGFP (Figure 5A,B,E) and resulted in rounded primordium morphology (Figure 5A,C) and stalled primordium migration (Figure 5A,D,E) 90 min after heat shock.
evidence: The text references multiple figures showing Cxcr4b-EGFP degradation and migration defects.

claim: After 120 min newly produced Cxcr4b-EGFP was detectable again and the primordium resumed its migration.
source: After 120 min newly produced Cxcr4b-EGFP was detectable again and the primordium resumed its migration (Figure 5A,E, Figure 5—Video 1).
evidence: The text references figures showing recovery of Cxcr4b-EGFP and migration.

claim: A pulse of zGrad expression can deplete Cxcr4b-EGFP to levels unable to sustain directed cell migration of the primordium.
source: Thus, a pulse of zGrad expression can deplete Cxcr4b-EGFP to levels unable to sustain directed cell migration of the primordium.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing transient migration defects.

claim: Temporal zGrad induction from the heat shock promoter can be used to induce reversible protein loss-of-function scenarios.
source: This suggests that temporal zGrad induction from the heat shock promoter can be used to induce reversible protein loss-of-function scenarios.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing reversible phenotypes.

claim: The expression pattern of zGrad mRNA in cxcr4b:zGrad embryos faithfully recapitulated the cxcr4b mRNA expression pattern.
source: The expression pattern of zGrad mRNA in cxcr4b:zGrad embryos faithfully recapitulated the cxcr4b mRNA expression pattern (Figure 6B).
evidence: The text references Figure 6B showing expression pattern comparison.

claim: zGrad efficiently depleted Cxcr4b-EGFP below detectable levels when expressed from the cxcr4b promoter.
source: This analysis showed that zGrad efficiently depleted Cxcr4b-EGFP below detectable levels (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The text references figures showing Cxcr4b-EGFP depletion.

claim: Embryos with the cxcr4b:zGrad transgene migrated on average only 72.5% of the distance.
source: In contrast, embryos with the cxcr4b:zGrad transgene migrated on average only 72.5% of the distance (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: The text references figures showing quantification of migration distance.

claim: Primordia in cxcr4b-/-; cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p1; cxcr4b:zGrad embryos migrated directionally but at reduced speed, did not fully complete their migration and failed to deposit the terminal neuromasts by 4 dpf.
source: Compared to primordia in cxcr4b-/- embryos, which showed little to no directed migration (Figure 6E,F) (Haas and Gilmour, 2006), primordia in cxcr4b-/-; cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p1; cxcr4b:zGrad embryos migrated directionally but at reduced speed, did not fully complete their migration and failed to deposit the terminal neuromasts by 4 dpf (Figure 6E,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The text references figures showing migration phenotypes and cites Haas and Gilmour, 2006.

claim: Expression of zGrad in the primordium did not affect its migration.
source: Importantly, expression of zGrad in the primordium did not affect its migration (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text references a figure showing normal migration with zGrad expression alone.

claim: zGrad expression from the cxcr4b promoter efficiently degrades Cxcr4b-EGFP to levels low enough to slow primordium migration but not low enough to recapitulate the primordium migration defect observed in embryos with loss of Cxcr4b function.
source: This suggests that zGrad expression from the cxcr4b promoter efficiently degrades Cxcr4b-EGFP to levels low enough to slow primordium migration but not low enough to recapitulate the primordium migration defect observed in embryos with loss of Cxcr4b function, probably because the cxcr4b promoter does not express zGrad at high enough levels for complete degradation of Cxcr4b-EGFP driven from the same promoter.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing partial phenotype and infers the mechanism.

claim: Expression of zGrad from a tissue-specific promoter can result in efficient degradation of GFP-tagged proteins to levels low enough to perturb protein function and cause tissue-specific defects.
source: More generally, these observations indicate that expression of zGrad from a tissue-specific promoter can result in efficient degradation of GFP-tagged proteins to levels low enough to perturb protein function and cause tissue-specific defects.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing tissue-specific phenotypes.

claim: zGrad rapidly degrades GFP-tagged proteins with half-lives of around 20 min for transmembrane and cytoplasmic proteins.
source: We found that zGrad rapidly degrades GFP-tagged proteins with half-lives of around 20 min for transmembrane and cytoplasmic proteins (Figure 2 and Table 1).
evidence: The text references Figure 2 and Table 1 showing degradation kinetics.

claim: The degradation of H2A-EGFP was significantly slower displaying a half-life of about 2.5 hr.
source: The degradation of H2A-EGFP was significantly slower displaying a half-life of about 2.5 hr (Figure 2 and Table 1).
evidence: The text references Figure 2 and Table 1 showing degradation kinetics.

claim: The slow degradation of H2A-EGFP could be due to the long life-time of histone proteins and the possibility that protein degradation is less efficient in nuclei.
source: This could be due to the long life-time of histone proteins (Clift et al., 2017) and the possibility that protein degradation is less efficient in nuclei.
evidence: This explanation is based on cited literature (Clift et al., 2017) and speculation.

claim: zGrad expression needs to be induced, which delays the onset of degradation by 65 to 200 min for the proteins investigated.
source: Importantly, in our system zGrad expression needs to be induced. This delays the onset of degradation by 65 to 200 min for the proteins we investigated.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing time to onset of degradation.

claim: zGrad degrades proteins rapidly enough to assess the consequences of abrupt protein inactivation.
source: Nevertheless, zGrad degrades proteins rapidly enough to assess the consequences of abrupt protein inactivation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing degradation kinetics.

claim: The AID system was combined with the deGradFP system by fusing AID to the vhhGFP4 anti-GFP nanobody and shown to degrade GFP-tagged proteins in an auxin-dependent manner in zebrafish.
source: Recently, the AID system was combined with the deGradFP system by fusing AID to the vhhGFP4 anti-GFP nanobody and shown to degrade GFP-tagged proteins in an auxin-dependent manner in zebrafish (Daniel et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement cites Daniel et al., 2018.

claim: The fusion of AID to the vhhGFP4 nanobody overcomes the leakiness observed with the AID system.
source: Also, the fusion of AID to the vhhGFP4 nanobody overcomes the leakiness that we observed with the AID system (Daniel et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement cites Daniel et al., 2018 and compares to their own observations.

claim: Compared to zGrad system, the mAID-nanobody system requires the expression of an additional component, the mAID-nanobody fusion protein.
source: However, compared to zGrad system, which requires the fusion of the protein of interest to GFP and the expression of zGrad, the mAID-nanobody system requires the expression of an additional component, the mAID-nanobody fusion protein – a feature that adds more versatility but also requires additional effort.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the design of the two systems.

claim: Depletion of maternal proteins by expressing zGrad from injected mRNA or as purified protein should uncover early protein requirements and can circumvent the laborious process of generating maternal mutants for essential genes by germline replacement.
source: Depletion of maternal proteins by expressing zGrad from injected mRNA or as purified protein should uncover early protein requirements and can circumvent the laborious process of generating maternal mutants for essential genes by germline replacement (Ciruna et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a proposed application based on experimental results and cites Ciruna et al., 2002.

claim: The depletion of maternal Ctnna results in an early and severe cell-cell adhesion defect.
source: Our finding that the depletion of maternal Ctnna results in an early and severe cell-cell adhesion defect is consistent with this idea (Figure 3).
evidence: The text references Figure 3 showing maternal Ctnna depletion phenotype.

claim: zGrad needs to be expressed at high enough levels to deplete proteins to sufficiently low levels to fully disrupt protein function.
source: An important consideration is that zGrad needs to be expressed at high enough levels to deplete proteins to sufficiently low levels to fully disrupt protein function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations of partial phenotypes.

claim: Systems such as Gal4/UAS or inducible systems such as the Tet-On system can be used to achieve high and tissue-specific zGrad expression.
source: One way to achieve high and tissue-specific zGrad expression is to amplify the production of zGrad through such systems as Gal4/UAS (Scheer and Campos-Ortega, 1999) or – to also add temporal control – inducible systems such as the Tet-On system (Campbell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed strategy citing relevant systems from Scheer and Campos-Ortega, 1999 and Campbell et al., 2012.

claim: zGrad should be a useful tool for the study of the consequences of acute loss-of-protein function in zebrafish, possibly also circumventing the problem of genetic compensation observed in studies of genetic mutants.
source: Such modifications combined with the increasing number of GFP-tagged transgenic (Trinh et al., 2011; Kawakami et al., 2010) and knock-in lines (Hoshijima et al., 2016) should render zGrad as a useful tool for the study of the consequences of acute loss-of-protein function in zebrafish, possibly also circumventing the problem of genetic compensation observed in studies of genetic mutants (Rossi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental results and cites multiple references (Trinh et al., 2011; Kawakami et al., 2010; Hoshijima et al., 2016; Rossi et al., 2015).

claim: zGrad recognizes different GFP versions (EGFP, sfGFP and Citrine).
source: It recognizes different GFP versions (EGFP, sfGFP and Citrine, Figures 1 and 2) and targets the tagged proteins for degradation.
evidence: The text references Figures 1 and 2 showing degradation of different GFP variants.

claim: Similar to deGradFP, zGrad degraded proteins tagged at the N-terminus, embedded within the protein and at the C-terminus.
source: In contrast to other degron systems (Natsume and Kanemaki, 2017) and similar to deGradFP (Caussinus et al., 2011), zGrad degraded proteins tagged at the N-terminus, embedded within the protein and at the C-terminus in the examples reported here (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: The text references figures and cites Natsume and Kanemaki, 2017 and Caussinus et al., 2011.

claim: The kinetics of zGrad-mediated degradation are similar to the kinetics reported for other degron-based systems.
source: These kinetics are similar to the kinetics reported for other degron-based systems (Daniel et al., 2018; Nishimura et al., 2009; Armenti et al., 2014).
evidence: This comparison cites Daniel et al., 2018; Nishimura et al., 2009; Armenti et al., 2014.

claim: The cxcr4b promoter drives expression in the somites and the posterior lateral line primordium.
source: Among other tissues, the cxcr4b promoter drives expression in the somites and the posterior lateral line primordium (primordium) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Chong et al., 2001).
evidence: The text references a figure and cites Chong et al., 2001.

claim: H2A-mCherry is not recognized by the anti-GFP nanobody and should not be subjected to zGrad-mediated protein degradation.
source: Since H2A-mCherry was expressed from the same promoter as H2A-EGFP and since H2A-mCherry is not recognized by the anti-GFP nanobody and should not be subjected to zGrad-mediated protein degradation (Caussinus et al., 2011), comparing the ratio of H2A-mCherry expression levels to H2A-EGFP should be a measure of H2A-EGFP in the absence of zGrad-mediated degradation.
evidence: This statement cites Caussinus et al., 2011 and explains the rationale for using mCherry as a control.

claim: The H2A-EGFP fluorescence intensity in the primordium was on average 3.8 times brighter than the H2A-EGFP fluorescence intensity in the somites.
source: Note that the H2A-EGFP fluorescence intensity in the primordium was on average 3.8 times brighter than the H2A-EGFP fluorescence intensity in the somites.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The H2A-mCherry fluorescence intensity in the primordium was on average 5.1 times brighter than the H2A-mCherry fluorescence intensity in the somites.
source: Note that the H2A-mCherry fluorescence intensity in the primordium was on average 5.1 times brighter than the H2A-mCherry fluorescence intensity in the somites.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The zGrad-mediated degradation of H2A-EGFP in the primordium is obscured by the continued production of H2A-EGFP.
source: †Note that the zGrad-mediated degradation of H2A-EGFP in the primordium is obscured by the continued production of H2A-EGFP.
evidence: This is stated in a footnote to Table 2.

claim: Cdh1 is required for cell-cell adhesion.
source: Second, we tested whether zGrad degrades transmembrane Cdh1-sfGFP efficiently enough to disrupt its function (Yoshida-Noro et al., 1984; Stephenson et al., 2010; Larue et al., 1994)
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and cites Yoshida-Noro et al., 1984; Stephenson et al., 2010; Larue et al., 1994.

claim: cdh1-/- embryos die during late gastrulation stages.
source: Such an analysis is currently not possible because cdh1-/- embryos die during late gastrulation stages (Kane et al., 1996; Kane et al., 2005; Montero et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement cites Kane et al., 1996; Kane et al., 2005; Montero et al., 2005.

claim: Cxcr4b functions as a guidance receptor for the migration of the primordium.
source: Third, we asked whether induction of zGrad can degrade the Sdf1 chemokine receptor Cxcr4b tagged with EGFP to temporarily disrupt its function as a guidance receptor for the migration of the primordium (Haas and Gilmour, 2006; David et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and cites Haas and Gilmour, 2006; David et al., 2002.

claim: Cxcr4b-EGFP expressed from the cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p7 transgene restores the migration of the primordium in cxcr4b-/- embryos.
source: Cxcr4b-EGFP expressed from the cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p7 transgene restores the migration of the primordium in cxcr4b-/- embryos and Kate2-CaaX expressed from an internal ribosomal entry site (IRES) serves as a marker for the primordium and an internal reference for how much Cxcr4b-EGFP is produced (Venkiteswaran et al., 2013; Lewellis et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement cites Venkiteswaran et al., 2013; Lewellis et al., 2013.

claim: The cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p1 fully restores primordium migration in cxcr4b mutant embryos.
source: Similar to the cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p7 transgenic line used above, the cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p1 fully restores primordium migration in cxcr4b mutant embryos, however, it expresses Cxcr4b-EGFP at two-fold lower levels (Fuentes et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement cites Fuentes et al., 2016.

claim: In cxcr4b mutant control embryos that carried the rescuing cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p1 transgene but lacked the cxcr4b:zGrad transgene, the primordium completed its migration and deposited the same number of neuromasts with the same spacing as in wild-type embryos.
source: In cxcr4b mutant control embryos that carried the rescuing cxcr4b:cxcr4b-EGFP-IRES-Kate2-CaaX-p1 transgene but lacked the cxcr4b:zGrad transgene, the primordium completed its migration and deposited the same number of neuromasts with the same spacing as in wild-type embryos (Figure 6E,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text references figures showing rescue of migration phenotype.

claim: Primordia in cxcr4b-/- embryos showed little to no directed migration.
source: Compared to primordia in cxcr4b-/- embryos, which showed little to no directed migration (Figure 6E,F) (Haas and Gilmour, 2006)
evidence: The text references figures and cites Haas and Gilmour, 2006.

claim: The observed phenotype in Z ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos injected with zGrad mRNA is similar to the defects reported for zygotic ctnna-/- embryos.
source: The observed phenotype in Z ctnna:ctnna-Citrine embryos injected with zGrad mRNA is similar to the defects reported for zygotic ctnna-/- embryos (Han et al., 2016).
evidence: This comparison cites Han et al., 2016.
